position: Monetary Rule Reform Options; Minimum Effective Reforms
proposal: The chapter recommends taking monetary discretion away from the Federal Reserve through free banking, commodity-backed money or a strict policy rule, presenting options in decreasing order of effectiveness: free banking, commodity-backed money, a K-percent money growth rule, inflation targeting, and inflation and growth targeting such as NGDP targeting or a Taylor rule (pp. 735-740). It says a K-percent rule may be the most feasible option and that the choice should ultimately be made through the lawmaking process (p. 740).
remaining: Any statutory monetary rule, commodity backing or free banking
Statement of an inflation target range by elected officials (tracked in c24-01)

status_summary: No bill establishing free banking, commodity-backed money, a K-percent rule or another statutory policy rule was found in the 119th Congress. The FOMC's Statement on Longer-Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy, revised 2025-08-22 and reaffirmed unchanged on 2026-01-28, keeps a 2 percent inflation goal, names the federal funds rate as the primary policy tool, contains no averaging language and references no policy or money growth rule. The gold-related bills seen (H.R. 3795 and S. 3218, Gold Reserve Transparency Act of 2025) concern reserve transparency, not a gold standard.

timeline.event: The FOMC released a revised Statement on Longer-Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy that keeps the 2 percent goal, drops averaging language and adopts no policy rule.
The FOMC reaffirmed the statement, identical to the August 2025 version, with no policy rule.
